sentences.text: What happened over the next three days was, Marit thinks now, the most interesting thing she has ever watched, and at the time she mostly found it embarrassing.
The village split, and it did not split the way you would expect.
It did not split old against young.
That was the thing that surprised her.
The Hansens, who were both over seventy, looked at the forecast and did nothing.

Kristian at the garage, who was twenty-six and had a tattoo of a wolf and who nobody would have picked, brought his mother's sheep down on the first afternoon and said, when asked, that his grandfather had been very clear with him about the hare and that he was not going to be the one who tested it.
It did not split by belief either.
Nobody in the village believed the hare was magic.

Marit asked several people directly, in the blunt way you can at twelve, and got six versions of the same answer: it is a hare, it goes white when it goes white, there is presumably a reason, the reason is presumably to do with light or cold or something in the ground.
The split was about something else, and it took her until she was much older to put a name on it.
She watched it happen over three days at the co-op, which was the only shop and therefore the whole of public life.
People came in and bought things, and what they bought told you where they stood.
Sacks.
Twine.
The particular blue tarpaulin.
Batteries, which was the tell, because batteries in the second week of October means somebody is expecting the power to go.
Nobody argued in the shop.
That was not how it was done.

What happened instead was that two people would meet at the till and one of them would have twine and the other would not, and there would be a fractional pause, and then they would talk about something else with great warmth for four minutes.
By the Wednesday the shop had run out of twine and had not run out of anything else, which told you the proportion better than any conversation.
Marit's mother did the seven days' work alone, in the evenings, without ever once asking Marit's father to help.
Marit helped.

She wants that recorded too, because at the time she told herself she was helping her mother and she has since worked out that she was hedging, and that hedging is the most common position in any argument of this kind and the one nobody ever admits to.
It was between the people who trusted a thing they could not explain because it had never failed, and the people who trusted a thing they could explain because they could explain it.
Her father was firmly in the second group and made an excellent case at every meal.
About half the village did the seven days' work.
The other half looked at the sky, which was mild, and at the leaves, which were on the trees, and got on with October.
